### Auto-regressive hidden Markov model

Let $x_{t}$ denote the six-dimensional vector of nose-head-body coordinates at video frame t (sampled at 80 Hz), with components $(x_{nose},y_{nose},x_{head},y_{head},x_{body},y_{body})$. We fit an AR-HMM to mouse trajectory data, ${x_{t}^{i}}$, across trials (indexed by i) from 13 out of 15 mice (two mice were excluded a priori due to low task performance). These mice performed olfactory search under the following experimental conditions: Variable ΔC, Constant |C| (nine mice); naris occlusion (seven mice); and Constant ΔC, Variable |C| experiments (five mice).

#### The generative view

Viewed as a generative model (that generates simulated data), the AR-HMM has two 'layers': a layer of hidden discrete states (corresponding to discrete movement motifs) and an observed layer that is the continuous trajectory $x_{t}$. We denote the temporal sequence of discrete states by $z_{t}$. In each time step, $z_{t}\in{1,2,…,S}$, that is, it is one of an S number of states, or movement motifs. The discrete hidden states evolve in time according to a Markov chain: going from time step t to t + 1, the discrete state may change to another state according to a transition probability matrix $\pi_{z_{1},z_{2}}$, which denotes the conditional probability of switching to $z_{2}$ having started in $z_{1}$. The probability distribution over the initial state, $z_{t=1}$, of the Markov chain at the start of each trial was taken to be the uniform distribution.

Now suppose for time steps $t_{1}$ to $t_{2}$ (inclusive) the discrete layer remained in state z. The continuous or auto-regressive (AR) part of the model dictates that, over this time interval, the continuous trajectory, $x_{t}$, evolves according to a linear AR process. The parameters of this AR process can be different in different states or motifs, z. In other words, $x_{t}$ is governed by

$$
x_{t}=A_{z}x_{t−1}+b_{z}+\epsilon_{t}.t_{1}\leqt\leqt_{2}
$$

where $A_{z}$ is a 6 × 6 matrix and b is a 6 × 1 vector, and the noise vector $\epsilon_{t}$ is sampled from the multi-variate zero-mean Gaussian distribution $N0,Q_{z}$, where $Q_{z}$ is a 6 × 6 noise covariance matrix. Moreover, the parameters $A_{z}$, $b_{z}$, and $Q_{z}$ depend on the discrete state z, and in general are different in different discrete states. The simple stochastic linear dynamics described by Equation (1) can describe simple motions of the mouse, such as turning left/right, dashing towards a certain direction, freezing (when $A_{z}$ is the identity matrix and $b_{z}$ is zero), etc. The switches between these simple behaviors allow the model to generate complex trajectories.

The AR-HMM is an example of a model with latent variables, which in this case are the discrete state sequence $z_{t}^{i}$ in each trial. The model, as a whole, is specified by the set of parameters ($\pi,{A_{z}},{b_{z}},{Q_{z}}$), which we will denote by $\theta$. For a d-dimensional trajectory (d = 6 here) and S states, comprises $SS-1+Sd^{2}+d+dd+1/2=SS-1+3dd+1/2$ parameters.

#### Model fits

Models with latent variables are often fit using the expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm, which maximizes the likelihood of the model in terms of the parameters $\theta≡\pi,{A_{z}},{b_{z}},{Q_{z}}$ for a given set of observed data ${x_{t}^{i}}$. In this work, we did not use the EM algorithm, but adopted a fully Bayesian approach in which both the hidden variables and the model parameters were inferred by drawing samples from their posterior distribution (Wiltschko et al., 2015). The posterior distribution combines the model likelihood and Bayesian priors imposed on its parameters, according to Bayes' rule. If we denote the joint likelihood of observed trajectories, ${x_{t}^{i}}$, and the latent variables, ${z_{t}^{i}}$, by $P{x_{t}^{i},z_{t}^{i}}\theta$ and the prior distribution over model parameters by $P\theta$, then up to normalization, the joint posterior distribution of latent variables and model parameters is given by

$$
P{z_{t}^{i}},\theta{x_{t}^{i}}∝P{x_{t}^{i},z_{t}^{i}}\thetaP\theta.
$$

For the AR-HMM, the (logarithm of the) joint log-likelihood is given by

$$
log⁡P{x_{t}^{i},z_{t}^{i}}\theta=\sum_{i}\sum_{t=2}^{T_{i}}[log⁡\pi_{z_{t-1}^{i},z_{t}^{i}}+logNx_{t}^{i}A_{z_{t}^{i}}x_{t-1}^{i}+b_{z_{t}^{i}},Q_{z_{t}^{i}}].
$$

where $T_{i}$ is the length of trial i, and we use the notation $Nx\mu,Q=e^{-\frac{1}{2}x-\mu^{T}Q^{-1}x-\mu}/\sqrt{2\piQ}$ to denote the density at point x of a multivariate Gaussian with mean vector μ and covariance matrix Q.

We imposed loose conjugate priors on the model parameters, which were factorized over the parameters of the AR process, ${A_{z}},{b_{z}},{Q_{z}}$, in different discrete states z, and the different rows of the Markov transition matrix, $\pi$. On the rows of $\pi$, we imposed Dirichlet distribution priors with uniform distribution means and concentration hyperparameter $\alpha$, which was set to 4. We imposed matrix normal inverse Wishart priors on the AR parameters, independently for different discrete states. Under this prior, the noise covariance $Q_{z}$ has an inverse Wishart distribution with a 'scale matrix' hyperparameter, which was set to the d × d ( = 6 × 6) identity matrix, and a 'degrees-of-freedom' scalar hyperparameter set to d + 2 = 8. Conditional on $Q_{z}$, the remaining AR parameters, $A_{z},b_{z}$, have a joint multivariate normal distribution under the prior, which can be specified by the prior mean and joint prior covariance matrix of $A_{z}$ and $b_{z}$. The prior means of $A_{z}$ and $b_{z}$ were set to the d × d identity matrix and the d-dimensional zero vector, respectively, while the prior covariance matrix of the concatenation $A_{z},b_{z}$ was given by the tensor product of $Q_{z}$ and the (d + 1) × (d + 1)( = 7 × 7) identity matrix (equivalently, under this prior, $b_{z}$ and different columns of $A_{z}$ are independent and uncorrelated, while each of these column vectors has a prior covariance equal to the [prior] AR noise covariance, $Q_{z}$).

Bayesian model inference was carried out by sampling from (instead of maximizing) the joint posterior distribution of the model parameters and latent state variables conditioned on the observed trajectory data (Equation 2). We did this by Gibbs sampling (an example of Markov chain Monte Carlo; not to be confused with the Markov chain in the AR-HMM), which works in a manner conceptually similar to the EM algorithm: it switches between sampling $z_{t}^{i}$ in all trials, conditioned on previously sampled parameters, and then sampling the parameters $\theta$ given the previous sample of ${z_{t}^{i}}$. To carry out this model inference procedure, we used the Python package developed by M.J. Johnson and colleagues, publicly available at https://github.com/mattjj/pyhsmm (Johnson et al., 2013a).

We ran the Gibbs sampler for 300 iterations and burned the first 200 samples, retaining 100. We used the remaining samples to obtain the posterior probabilities of hidden discrete states at each time step of each trial (by calculating the frequency of different state in that time step and trial, across the retained Gibbs samples), as well as posterior expectation of the model parameters (by calculating their averages over the retained Gibbs samples). We refer to the AR-HMM with parameters given by these latter posterior expectations as the ‘fit model’.

#### Model selection

We fit AR-HMM's with different numbers of states (motifs), S, to mouse trajectory data pooled across animals. To evaluate the statistical goodness of fit of these fit model and select the best S (the number of states or motifs), we evaluated the log-likelihoods of fit models on trajectory data from a held-out set of trials, not used for model fitting. The corresponding plot of log-likelihoods is shown in Figure 6F. As seen, the log-likelihood keeps increasing with S, up to S = 100. This shows that, up to at least S = 100, additional motifs do have utility in capturing more variability in mouse trajectories. These variabilities may include differences in movement across mice, as well as movement variations in the same mouse but across different trials or different instances of the same movement; for example, a clockwise head turn executed with different speeds in different instances or trials. In the AR-HMM, the AR observation distribution of a given Markov state corresponds to a very simple (linear) dynamical system that cannot capture many natural and continuous variations in movement, such as changes in movement speed. Nevertheless, AR-HMM models with higher S can capture such variations with more precision by specializing different discrete Markov states, with different AR distributions, to movement motifs of different mice, or, for example, to capture different speeds of the same qualitative movement motif.

The goal for this modeling was to give a compact description of recurring movement features across animals and conditions, suitable for visualization and alignment. For these purposes, the goodness of fit did not provide a suitable criterion because the log-likelihood plots did not peak or plateau even at very large numbers of states. Guided by visual inspection, we thus chose the model with S = 16 for the main figures (Figures 6–8). Although this was a somewhat arbitrary choice, we show that the findings in Figures 6–8 do not depend on the choice of S – models with S = 6, 10, or 20 gave equivalent results (Figure 6—figure supplements 2–4).

#### MAP sequences

The Gibbs sampling algorithm that we used for model inference yields (time-wise marginal) maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimates of the latent variables ${z_{t}^{i}}$, as follows. Using the Gibbs samples for the latent variables, we can estimate the posterior probability of the mouse being in any of the S states in any given time step of a given trial. We made MAP sequences by picking, at any time step and trial, the state with the highest posterior probability. The inferred MAP motifs tended to have high posterior probability, which exceeded 0.8 in 66.2% of all time steps across the 17,195 trials in the modeled dataset.

### Decoding analysis

We decoded experimental conditions and animal identities from single-trial MAP motif sequences inferred using the AR-HMM. Specifically, we trained multi-class decoders with linear decision boundaries (linear discriminant analysis) to decode the above categorical variables from the single-trial empirical state transition probability matrices derived from the MAP sequence of each trial. If $z_{t}^{(i)}^$ is the motif MAP sequence for trial i, the empirical transition probability, $\pi_{a,b}^{(i)}^$, from state a to state $ba,b\in{1,…,K}$, for that trial was calculated by

$$
\pi_{a,b}^{(i)}^≡\frac{n_{a,b}^{(i)}}{\sumc=1Kn_{a,c}^{(i)}}.
$$



$$
n_{a,b}^{(i)}≡\sumt=1T^{(i)}−1I(z_{t}^=a)I(z_{t+1}^=b).
$$

where $T^{i}$ is the length of trial i, and $I⋅$ is an indicator function, returning 1 or 0 when its argument is true or false, respectively.

We used the decoder to either classify experimental condition or mouse identity, in different trials (Figure 6D, E). For decoders trained to classify the trials' experimental condition, we used pooled data across mice. For decoders trained to classify mouse identity, we only used data from the 80:20 odor condition. Data was split into training and test dataset in a stratified fivefold cross-validation manner, ensuring equal proportions of trials of different types in both datasets. The trial type was the combination of left vs. right decision, experimental condition, and mouse identity.

To calculate the statistical significance of decoding accuracies, we performed an iterative shuffle procedure on each fold of the cross-validation. In each shuffle, the training labels that the classifier was trained to decode were shuffled randomly across trials of the training set, and the classifier's accuracy was evaluated on the unshuffled test dataset. This shuffle was performed 100 times to create a shuffle distribution of decoding accuracies for each fold of the cross-validation. From these distributions, we calculated the z-score of decoding accuracy for each class in each cross-validation fold. These z-scores were then averaged across the folds of cross-validation and used to calculate the overall p-value of the decoding accuracy obtained on the original data.

Reviewer #2:

In this study, Smear et al. aim to investigate how mice sample the noisy stimulus information from olfactory plumes such as to navigate towards their source. To this end, they developed a 2AFC task for freely moving mice where the same odor emanates from two lateral sources, at independently controllable concentrations. Mice are required to identify the more intense of the two sources and collect water from reward port located on the side with the higher odor concentration. The authors improve on previous attempts at studying this problem by requiring the mice to commit to their decision at a substantial distance from the odor ports. This forces the mice to assess odor concentration from distal cues rather than via serial sampling of the sources themselves. Interestingly, the authors find that stereo olfaction (comparing concentration across two nostrils) is not required to determine source location from distal cues. Using a series of stimulus conditions, the authors convincingly show that in their paradigm, mice rely on olfactory cues and specifically the relative, not absolute, concentration difference between the two sources.

The relevance of stereo olfaction for airborne odor cues has been long debated. In my opinion, the authors results in principle resolve this debate – stereo comparisons allow finer source localisation near the source, while serial sampling may play a larger role farther away from source. One concern however is that this lack of reliance on stereo sampling may result from the specific task design and the constraints it imposes on the behavior (see concerns).

Further, the authors characterise the sampling behaviors of mice during this task by monitoring respiration (thermistor) as well as nose, head and body positions (video tracking). The authors find a striking, active synchronisation of sniffing and nose (and body) movements that gets selectively recruited during putative investigatory phase of the task i.e. when mice are actively exploring the concentration gradient. The authors do exhaustive analysis to show that such synchronisation is not a default state and the coupling is much weaker during other phases within the same trial. While such coupling of movement and intrinsic rhythms has been proposed previously, to my knowledge this is the first careful characterisation of this phenomenon in freely moving mice. Importantly, the authors results not only confirm the existence of such coupling but also clarify that this synchronisation is an active feature of olfactory navigation. Interestingly however, the authors do not find any significant difference in sampling strategies across different stimulus difficulties (see concerns).

Lastly, the authors use machine learning to parse motion trajectories into identifiable behavioral motifs. With their approach, they find that a range of motifs that are stereotyped across mice and occur in non-random sequences during each trial. Further, a trained decoder can successfully decode mouse identity from the sequences in which these motifs in each animal. While these motif based analysis are well done, the data presented do not seem to make any clear predictions about how these motif sequences would change in different task conditions. The authors do not find any obvious relationship between trial types (difficult versus easy stimuli) and motif sequences and the presented analyses do not add much to the main message of the paper. I therefore lack the imagination to accurately assess the relevance of this portion of the study.

Overall, the study is well executed – the data presented are clear with numerous controls at each step. In my opinion, the evidence provided for lack of need for stereo olfaction for distal source assessment and active synchronisation of sniffing and sampling movements are important contributions to the field of olfaction that warrant publication in eLife. However, I have several conceptual concern about the task design and the interpretations of the results that the authors should clarify prior to publication.

1. My primary concern is about the task design. I commend the authors for the careful control of olfactory stimuli and substantial improvements over previously published odor localisation assays by separating the reward port from the odor source and forcing decisions at locations distant from the source. However, the task design chosen does not really require the mice to localize odor sources beyond just indicating whether there is more odor on the right versus left. This is different from natural conditions, where the necessary spatial resolution may be much higher. In fact, finer source localization confers no additional benefit for maximizing reward in this task. Therefore, the sampling strategies exhibited by the subjects here may be different from those employed during natural odor navigation where the motivation is to precisely locate the source of mate, food or predators.

2. Along the same lines, it is surprising that even for the easiest version of the task, the performance hovers around 80%, even though PID characterisations show very clear differences between the two halves of the arena. Furthermore, performance drops with increasing stimulus difficulty but mice do not appear to change their sampling strategies to compensate for the lower reward rate. I am trying to reconcile these two facts. At first pass, given known olfactory acuity of rodents, it seems that trained mice should have no trouble handling the easiest stimuli (reach almost 100% success). One possibility is that the mice are not fully motivated/engaged in the task. An alternate explanation is that mice are fully motivated to reach maximum reward rate, but the task is just too hard and the sampling strategies employed at 100:0 condition are their best, and therefore with increasing stimulus difficulty, they cannot perform any better. Yet, the latter possibility appears very unlikely. Can the authors comment on these two possibilities? The question remains whether mice when pushed to achieve higher performances would employ different sampling strategies.

3. Lastly, looking at Figure 5Ai it appears that overall nose speeds are significantly lower during ITI than during the investigatory bouts within the trial. While the authors rule out that sniffing-movement synchronisation is simply a feature of rapid sniffing, they do not rule out the dependence on running speeds. Perhaps the apparent lack of synchrony in ITI results from poorer ability to resolve decelerations, given lower speeds on average. This is also consistent with reduced, but significant synchrony during premature initiations in the ITI (Figure S7A) where speeds tend to be higher than those shown in Figure 5Ai. This should be easily addressable by repeating the analysis on speed matched datasets.

Together with panel 3D, it suggests that mice undergo fairly stereotyped searches: after poking their nose out of the initiation port, they appear to make a 180 degree rotation (sweep) to face the gradient. The density reaches a maximum at that point (opposite to the position of the initiation port). Is this position (crossing of the alpha shape) dominated by an "investigation" state? Can this position be viewed as a decision point? When/where does the animal tend switch to the "approach" state? More generally, could you map dominate trends in behavioral motifs of Figure 6B onto the stereotyped alpha shape of the occupancy diagram of Figure 3F?

3. Figure 2D: Could you speculate about the reason why trials tend to be longer for the 100:0 conditions compared to the more difficult 60:40? Do mice spend more time in the investigation phase when gradient is stronger? Although this result would be counter-intuitive, it might suggest that mice learn (?) to spend less time on the initial search when less information is available to them.

4. Figure 1D indicates that the average gradient's geometry is not the same when the odor is delivered on the left side (100:0) compared to the right side (0:100). This observation appears to be true for the other odor ratios reported in Figure S2. This asymmetry should affect the gradient that the animal experiences during the investigation phase, which should in turn influence the accuracy of the decisions. Do you expect a 50:50 condition to produce no preference (on average)?

5. Figure 7F: What are you concluding from this panel? Are you sure that the shaded areas represent the standard deviation and not the SEM? If the standard deviation is shown, how do you explain the existence of stereotypical wiggles on a timescale of 50 ms? It would be very useful to represent a variant of Figure 7C where the trials are sorted between correct and incorrect.

claims.claim: Mice solve the olfactory search task using concentration gradient cues.

claims.claim: Mice do not require stereo olfaction for performance in the olfactory search task.
claims.source: Mice solve this task using concentration gradient cues and do not require stereo olfaction for performance.
claims.evidence: Naris occlusion experiments (Figure 2F) showed no significant impact on performance, indicating stereo olfaction is not necessary.

claims.claim: Respiration and nose movement are synchronized with tens of milliseconds precision during task performance.

claims.claim: Sniff-synchronized nose movement is present during trials and largely absent during inter-trial intervals.

claims.claim: Sniff-synchronized nose movement is a strategic behavioral state rather than a constant accompaniment to fast breathing.

claims.claim: The allocentric structure of investigation and approach indicates an advantage to sampling both sides of the sharpest part of the odor gradient.

claims.claim: Navigating by chemical cues may be one of the most ancient problems motile organisms evolved to solve.
claims.source: Navigating by chemical cues may be one of the most ancient problems motile organisms evolved to solve, and it remains crucial in the lives of almost all modern species.
claims.evidence: This is a statement drawing from established scientific knowledge about the evolutionary importance of chemotaxis.

claims.claim: Chemical gradient navigation remains crucial in the lives of almost all modern species.
claims.source: Navigating by chemical cues may be one of the most ancient problems motile organisms evolved to solve, and it remains crucial in the lives of almost all modern species.
claims.evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the widespread importance of chemosensory navigation.

claims.claim: Unicellular organisms and some invertebrates navigate chemical gradients by chemotaxis.
claims.source: Unicellular organisms and some invertebrates navigate chemical gradients by chemotaxis (Bargmann, 2006; Berg, 2000; Lockery, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Chemotaxis movement programs can be described as having two states: moving straight when concentration is increasing and reorienting when concentration is decreasing.
claims.source: In essence, their movement programs can be described as having two states: they move straight when the concentration is increasing and reorient their movements when the concentration is decreasing.
claims.evidence: This describes established knowledge about chemotaxis behavior patterns.

claims.claim: For many larger or flying organisms, odor gradient cues do not provide useful positional information at their spatial scale.
claims.source: Whereas chemical gradients are stable and informative at the spatial scale of these organisms, for many larger or flying organisms, odor gradient cues do not provide useful positional information (Crimaldi et al., 2002; Murlis et al., 1992; Baker et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on turbulent odor plumes.

claims.claim: Turbulent airflow moves odor molecules in dynamic spatiotemporal patterns, disrupting concentration gradients.
claims.source: At this larger spatial scale, turbulent airflow moves odor molecules in dynamic spatiotemporal patterns, disrupting concentration gradients and nullifying classical chemotaxis strategies.
claims.evidence: This describes established knowledge about turbulent flow effects on odor plumes.

claims.claim: In odor-gated anemotaxis, odor cues gate behavioral responses to positional information provided by another modality.
claims.source: In this behavioral program, known as odor-gated anemotaxis, odor cues gate behavioral responses to positional information provided by another modality.
claims.evidence: This describes a known behavioral strategy in insects, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Novel odors evoke rapid sniffing in rodents.
claims.source: Novel odors evoke rapid sniffing, during which respiration synchronizes with whisker, nose, and head movements on a cycle-by-cycle basis (Kurnikova et al., 2017; Moore et al., 2013; Ranade et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: During rapid sniffing evoked by novel odors, respiration synchronizes with whisker, nose, and head movements on a cycle-by-cycle basis.
claims.source: Novel odors evoke rapid sniffing, during which respiration synchronizes with whisker, nose, and head movements on a cycle-by-cycle basis (Kurnikova et al., 2017; Moore et al., 2013; Ranade et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Rodents follow odor trails with rapid sniffing accompanied by side-to-side head movements.
claims.source: Previous work has shown that rodents follow odor trails, where the concentration gradient is steep and stable, with rapid sniffing accompanied by side-to-side head movements (Jones and Urban, 2018; Khan et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Serial sniffing and stereo olfactory cues guide movements of the nose during odor trail following.
claims.source: In these conditions, serial sniffing and stereo olfactory cues guide movements of the nose.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies on odor trail following behavior.

claims.claim: Moles used concentration comparisons across space and time to locate a food source in a sealed experimental chamber.
claims.source: Likewise, moles used concentration comparisons across space and time to locate a food source in a sealed experimental chamber in which a lack of airflow allowed for even diffusion of a chemical gradient (Catania, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Catania, 2013.

claims.claim: When input to the nares was reversed in moles, they navigated towards odor sources at a distance but demonstrated significant deficits at identifying odor location when near the source.
claims.source: In this study, when input to the nares was reversed, moles navigated towards odor sources at a distance, but demonstrated significant deficits at identifying odor location when near the source.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Catania, 2013.

claims.claim: Inter-naris concentration comparison plays a more important role in search near the source.
claims.source: Behavioral modeling in mice further supports that inter-naris concentration comparison plays a more important role in search near the source (Liu et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claims.claim: In previous experiments where rodents searched in airborne odor plumes, mice developed a memory-based strategy of serially sampling each possible reward location.
claims.source: In previous experiments where rodents searched in airborne odor plumes, mice developed a memory-based strategy of serially sampling each possible reward location for the presence of odor, turning search tasks into detection tasks (Bhattacharyya and Bhalla, 2015; Gire et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Mice learn the olfactory search task rapidly and robustly.
claims.source: Mice learn the olfactory search task rapidly and robustly.
claims.evidence: Figure 2B shows that almost all mice performed above chance in the first session, with most exceeding 80% performance within four sessions.

claims.claim: Almost all mice performed above chance in the first session of the 100:0 condition.
claims.source: Almost all mice performed above chance in the first session (Figure 2B; binomial test, p<0.05 for 24 out of 25 mice, 75 ± 9.2% correct, mean ± sd).
claims.evidence: Statistical testing (binomial test) on behavioral data from Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Within four sessions of the 100:0 condition, most animals exceeded 80% performance.
claims.source: Within four sessions, most animals exceeded 80% performance (19 out of 26).
claims.evidence: Behavioral performance data from training sessions.

claims.claim: Mice trained to search pinene plumes generalize their search behavior to vanillin, a novel odorant.
claims.source: We found no differences in performance between vanillin and pinene sessions for these mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A; Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=0.827, n = 3).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of performance between pinene and vanillin conditions.

claims.claim: Vanillin does not activate the trigeminal fibers of the nose.
claims.source: We chose vanillin as the novel odorant because, unlike pinene, vanillin does not activate the trigeminal fibers of the nose (Cometto-Muñiz and Abraham, 2010; Doty et al., 1978; Hummel et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Search behavior in the olfactory task does not rely on the trigeminal system.
claims.source: These data suggest that this search behavior generalizes across odors and does not rely on the trigeminal system.
claims.evidence: Inference from the vanillin experiment showing equivalent performance without trigeminal activation.

claims.claim: On odor omission probe trials, mice performed at chance.
claims.source: On these probe trials, mice performed at chance (binomial test, p=0.9989), with longer trial durations (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05) and more tortuous trajectories (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05) than on non-probe trials (Figure 2C; n = 19, all data from 80:20 condition with probe trials).
claims.evidence: Statistical testing on behavioral data from odor omission trials.

claims.claim: Odor omission trials resulted in longer trial durations compared to non-probe trials.
claims.source: On these probe trials, mice performed at chance (binomial test, p=0.9989), with longer trial durations (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05) and more tortuous trajectories (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05) than on non-probe trials (Figure 2C; n = 19, all data from 80:20 condition with probe trials).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of trial durations between probe and non-probe trials.

claims.claim: Odor omission trials resulted in more tortuous trajectories compared to non-probe trials.
claims.source: On these probe trials, mice performed at chance (binomial test, p=0.9989), with longer trial durations (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05) and more tortuous trajectories (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05) than on non-probe trials (Figure 2C; n = 19, all data from 80:20 condition with probe trials).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of path tortuosity between probe and non-probe trials.

claims.claim: Performance drops with decreasing concentration ratio.
claims.source: Performance drops with the concentration ratio (ΔC), consistent with our reasoning that mice would use odor gradient cues in this task (Figure 2D; pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, p<0.05, n = 15).
claims.evidence: Statistical analysis of performance across different concentration ratios (100:0, 80:20, 60:40).

claims.claim: Varying the concentration ratio from 80:20 to 60:40 did not affect trial duration or path tortuosity.
claims.source: Varying the concentration ratio from 80:20 to 60:40 did not affect trial duration or path tortuosity, defined as actual path length divided by direct path length (Figure 2D; pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, p>0.05).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of trial duration and tortuosity across concentration ratios.

claims.claim: Trial duration and path tortuosity were slightly but statistically significantly longer in the 100:0 condition compared to other conditions.
claims.source: However, trial duration and path tortuosity were slightly, but statistically significantly, longer in the 100:0 condition (pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of behavioral metrics across concentration conditions.

claims.claim: Equal performance in 90:30 and 30:10 conditions indicates that mice are guided by odor gradients rather than using an intensity judgment strategy.
claims.source: These results indicate that odor gradients guide olfactory search under these conditions.
claims.evidence: Inference from the equal performance in conditions where intensity judgment would produce different outcomes.

claims.claim: Naris occlusion did not significantly impact performance or path tortuosity.
claims.source: We found that naris occlusion did not significantly impact performance or path tortuosity (pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum tests, p>0.05).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of performance and tortuosity across naris occlusion conditions.

claims.claim: Naris occlusion resulted in a slight but statistically significant increase in trial duration compared to the no-stitch condition.
claims.source: When compared with the no-stitch condition, the naris stitch condition resulted in a slight, but statistically significant, increase in trial duration (pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of trial duration between naris stitch and no-stitch conditions.

claims.claim: The increase in trial duration with naris occlusion may be a result of undergoing a surgical procedure rather than the occlusion itself.
claims.source: This is not true when the stitch condition is compared with the sham condition (pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p>0.05), indicating this may be a result of undergoing a surgical procedure.
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison showing no difference between stitch and sham conditions.

claims.claim: Stereo comparison is not necessary in the olfactory search task.
claims.source: These overall results indicate that stereo comparison is not necessary in this task (Figure 2F; n = 13), and that temporal comparisons across sniffs (Catania, 2013; Parabucki et al., 2019) play a larger role under our task conditions.
claims.evidence: Inference from naris occlusion experiments showing no performance deficit.

claims.claim: Temporal comparisons across sniffs play a larger role than stereo comparisons under the task conditions.
claims.source: These overall results indicate that stereo comparison is not necessary in this task (Figure 2F; n = 13), and that temporal comparisons across sniffs (Catania, 2013; Parabucki et al., 2019) play a larger role under our task conditions.
claims.evidence: Inference from naris occlusion results combined with citations to prior work on temporal comparisons.

claims.claim: The overall sniff pattern was consistent across trials.
claims.source: The overall sniff pattern was consistent across trials, with an inhalation just before trial initiation followed by a long exhalation or pause at the beginning of the trial (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: Figure 3A shows consistent sniff patterns across trials.

claims.claim: Mice performed a rapid burst of sniffs after trial initiation, then sniffed more slowly as they approached the target.

claims.evidence: Figure 3A shows temporal dynamics of sniff rate during trials.

claims.claim: Inhalation and sniff durations were shorter during trials than during inter-trial intervals.
claims.source: In this active behavioral state, inhalation and sniff durations were shorter during trials than during ITIs (p<<0.01 for all mice; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test; Figure 3B, C)
claims.evidence: Statistical comparison of sniff parameters between trials and ITIs shown in Figure 3B, C.

claims.claim: Sniff durations during the task are strikingly shorter than those observed in head-fixed rodents.
claims.source: In this active behavioral state, inhalation and sniff durations were shorter during trials than during ITIs (p<<0.01 for all mice; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test; Figure 3B, C), and strikingly shorter than those observed in head-fixed rodents (Bolding and Franks, 2017; Shusterman et al., 2011; Wesson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Comparison with cited literature on head-fixed rodent sniffing.

claims.claim: The across-mouse mean occupancy distribution was evenly distributed across the two sides of the arena.
claims.source: Although individual mice showed position biases (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), these biases were not systematic across mice, so that the across-mouse mean occupancy distribution was evenly distributed across the two sides of the arena (Figure 3F; n = 19).

claims.claim: Sniff rate was highest near the initiation port and slower on the approach to target.
claims.source: Consistent with this sniffing and movement pattern, the sniff rate was highest near the initiation port and slower on the approach to target (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: Figure 3G shows spatial distribution of sniff rate.

claims.claim: Measures of active sampling were not statistically distinguishable across gradient or naris occlusion conditions.
claims.source: These measures of active sampling were not statistically distinguishable across gradient or naris occlusion conditions, but changed significantly on odor omission probe trials, with more fast sniffing and head turns overall.

claims.claim: On odor omission probe trials, there was more fast sniffing and head turns overall.
claims.source: These measures of active sampling were not statistically distinguishable across gradient or naris occlusion conditions, but changed significantly on odor omission probe trials, with more fast sniffing and head turns overall.

claims.claim: Nose speed accelerates during exhalation, peaks at inhalation onset, and decelerates during inhalation.

claims.evidence: Figure 5Aii shows sniff-aligned yaw velocity dynamics.

claims.claim: Z-velocity reaches peak upward velocity at inhalation onset, decelerates and goes downward during inhalation, and rises again at exhalation.
claims.source: The Z-velocity reaches peak upward velocity at inhalation onset, decelerates and goes downward during inhalation, and rises again at exhalation (Figure 5Aiii).
claims.evidence: Figure 5Aiii shows sniff-aligned Z-velocity dynamics.

claims.evidence: Analysis controlling for nose speed shows persistent differences in synchrony.

claims.claim: Sniff-synchronized movement is not an inevitable biomechanical accompaniment to fast sniffing, but rather reflects a strategic behavioral state.

claims.claim: After premature attempts at trial initiation, mice execute sniff-synchronized movement despite the absence of experimenter-applied odor stimulus.

claims.claim: Sniff synchrony changes dramatically between crossing the decision line and entering the reward port.

claims.evidence: Figure 7C, D show temporal structure of investigation and approach states.

claims.claim: Switches from approach back to investigation were common during trials.

claims.claim: Mice are continuously integrating evidence about the odor gradient throughout their trajectory to the target.
claims.source: This pattern suggests that the mice are continuously integrating evidence about the odor gradient throughout their trajectory to the target.
claims.evidence: Inference from the observation of frequent switches between investigation and approach states.

claims.evidence: Figure 7E shows differences in nose speed and sniff rate between investigation and approach.

claims.claim: Sniff-synchronized kinematic rhythms were distinct in investigation and approach states.
claims.source: Third, the sniff-synchronized kinematic rhythms (Figures 4 and 5) were distinct in the two states (Figure 7F; Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p<0.01).
claims.evidence: Figure 7F shows differential kinematic modulation between states with statistical testing.

claims.claim: Nose speed and yaw velocity are more synchronized with sniffing during the investigation state.

claims.claim: Motif transition times indicate 'decision points' at which the animal chooses its next move.

claims.claim: The overlap region between investigation and approach occupancy is displaced toward the chosen side of the arena in all individual mice.

claims.claim: Correct trials feature significantly increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of the midline relative to incorrect trials.

results.result: Mice use concentration gradient cues to solve the olfactory search task. Performance decreases with decreasing concentration ratio (ΔC) while remaining constant when absolute concentration varies but gradient is held constant, demonstrating gradient-guided rather than intensity-based navigation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C34, C38, and C106 are well-supported by experimental data showing performance varies with gradient magnitude (Figure 2D) but not with absolute concentration when gradient is constant (Figure 2E, 90:30 vs 30:10 conditions). Statistical tests confirm these differences, and the experimental design appropriately controls for alternative strategies.

results.result: Stereo olfaction is not necessary for task performance; mice rely primarily on temporal comparisons across sniffs. Naris occlusion did not significantly impact performance or path tortuosity, though trial duration showed a small increase attributable to surgical procedure rather than occlusion itself.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C39, C42, and C43 are supported by naris occlusion experiments (Figure 2F) with appropriate statistical controls including sham surgery. The inference that temporal comparisons play a larger role (C43) is reasonable given the lack of stereo deficit, though direct evidence for temporal comparison mechanisms is cited rather than demonstrated.

results.result: Respiration and nose movement are synchronized with tens of milliseconds precision during task performance. Nose speed peaks at inhalation onset, yaw velocity reaches peak centrifugal velocity at inhalation, and Z-velocity shows coordinated modulation with the sniff cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C52-C55 are well-supported by kinematic data in Figure 5 showing precise temporal alignment between movement parameters and sniffing. Statistical validation against shuffled controls (C55, p<0.001) confirms these modulations exceed chance expectations. The temporal precision is directly demonstrated in the data.

results.result: Sniff-synchronized nose movement is a strategic behavioral state selectively deployed during task performance. This synchrony is present during trials but largely absent during inter-trial intervals, even when controlling for movement speed, and appears during premature initiation attempts despite absence of odor.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 and C56-C61 are supported by differential kinematic synchrony between trial and ITI periods (Figure 5), with controls for movement speed (C57, Figure 5—supplement 2). The observation during premature initiations (C59) and post-decision changes (C60) provide additional evidence for strategic deployment. The inference of proactive strategy (C61) is well-justified by converging evidence.

results.result: Movement motifs cluster into two behavioral states—investigation and approach—based on transition probabilities. Investigation motifs occur early in trials while approach motifs occur later, though frequent switches between states indicate continuous evidence integration rather than ballistic commitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7 and C67-C71 are supported by clustering analysis of transition probability matrix (Figure 7A) and temporal distribution of motif onsets (Figure 7B-D). The observation of frequent state switches (C70) directly supports the inference of continuous integration (C71). The analysis appropriately uses unsupervised methods to identify structure.

results.result: Investigation motif onsets are precisely locked to specific phases of the sniff cycle. All investigation motifs show significant modulation in both time and phase coordinates relative to sniffing, while approach motifs show weaker or absent modulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C76-C77, and C95 are supported by motif-sniff alignment analysis (Figure 8) with statistical validation via permutation tests (p<0.001 for investigation motifs). The differential modulation between investigation and approach states is clearly demonstrated. The analysis appropriately distinguishes time vs. phase coordination.

results.result: Mice sample both sides of the steepest part of the odor gradient, consistent with a serial-sniff strategy. Correct trials feature significantly increased investigation at and across the midline where gradients are steepest, rather than downwind where absolute concentrations are highest.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 and C84-C85 are supported by occupancy analysis showing correct trials have increased investigation on the unchosen side of midline (Figure 10G, p<0.001). The spatial pattern matches gradient discriminability maps (Figure 1—supplement 2D) rather than absolute concentration maps (Figure 1—supplement 2C), supporting serial-sniff interpretation. Controls for stay/switch trials (C87-C88) strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: Investigation and approach states differ in movement speed, sniff rate, and kinematic synchrony. Investigation involves slower movement with faster sniffing and stronger sniff-synchronized kinematics, particularly for nose speed and yaw velocity.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 are supported by state-specific analysis (Figure 7E-F) with statistical validation (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p<0.01). Shuffle controls confirm nose speed and yaw velocity modulation exceeds across-trial tendencies (p<0.001), though Z-velocity does not (p=0.31). The differential characterization of states is well-established.

results.result: The spatial location of investigation matters for performance. Correct trials show increased investigation in the transition zone (5-10 cm from initiation), while increased investigation near the decision line is associated with incorrect trials, indicating location-dependent utility of investigation behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 are supported by longitudinal analysis of investigation-approach index (Figure 10C, p<0.001). The location-dependent relationship between investigation and performance is clearly demonstrated, supporting the inference that investigation is not uniformly beneficial (C83). Statistical validation via permutation tests is appropriate.

results.result: Mice learn the olfactory search task rapidly and robustly. Almost all mice (24/25) performed above chance in the first session of 100:0 training, with most (19/26) exceeding 80% performance within four sessions.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 are supported by training data (Figure 2B) with appropriate statistical testing (binomial test, p<0.05). Sample sizes are adequate (n=25-26 mice) and performance criteria are clearly defined. The rapid learning is well-documented.

results.result: Search behavior generalizes to novel odorants and does not rely on the trigeminal system. Mice trained on pinene showed equivalent performance with vanillin, which does not activate trigeminal fibers.
results.evaluation: Claims C28 and C30 are supported by comparison of pinene and vanillin performance (Figure 2—supplement 2A, p=0.827). However, sample size is small (n=3), limiting confidence. Claim C29 about vanillin's trigeminal properties is supported by citations but not directly tested. The generalization conclusion is reasonable but would benefit from larger sample size.

results.result: On odor omission probe trials, mice performed at chance with longer trial durations and more tortuous trajectories compared to odor-present trials. Active sampling increased during omission trials with more fast sniffing and head turns.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 and C51 are supported by odor omission data (Figure 2C) with appropriate statistical tests (binomial test for chance performance, Wilcoxon rank-sum for duration and tortuosity, p<0.05). These results confirm odor-dependence of performance and reveal compensatory sampling strategies.

results.result: Sniff patterns are consistent across trials, featuring an inhalation before initiation, rapid burst of sniffs early in trial, then slower sniffing approaching target. Sniff durations during task are shorter than in inter-trial intervals and strikingly shorter than in head-fixed rodents.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 and C49 are supported by sniff analysis (Figure 3A-C, G) with statistical validation (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p<<0.01). Comparison with head-fixed literature (C47) is appropriately cited. The characterization of sniff dynamics is thorough and well-documented.

results.result: Movement motif sequences can decode individual mouse identity (8/9 mice above chance) but do not distinguish between concentration gradients. Only odor omission trials produce distinguishable motif patterns, suggesting mice do not modify sampling behavior in a gradient-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 and C93 are supported by linear classifier analysis (Figure 6D-E) with appropriate statistical validation (p<0.01). The inability to decode gradient conditions despite successful mouse identification indicates the model captures individual differences but not stimulus-dependent modulation. The inference about lack of gradient-dependent modification (C66) is justified.

results.result: Movement trajectories vary considerably across trials and are not stereotyped. Individual mice show position biases, but these are not systematic across mice, resulting in even occupancy distribution across arena sides at the population level.
results.evaluation: Claims C48 and C92 are supported by occupancy analysis (Figure 3D-F, Figure 3—supplement 1). The observation of individual biases that cancel at population level is clearly demonstrated. This variability motivates the unsupervised modeling approach used in subsequent analyses.

results.result: Trial duration and path tortuosity did not differ between 80:20 and 60:40 conditions, though both were slightly longer in 100:0 condition. Active sampling measures were not distinguishable across gradient or naris occlusion conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C36 and C50 are supported by behavioral metrics analysis (Figure 2D) with appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon rank-sum). The lack of differences between some conditions is properly reported with p>0.05. The small but significant difference in 100:0 (C36) is noted appropriately.

results.result: When trials are oriented by choice, the overlap region between investigation and approach occupancy is displaced toward the chosen side in all individual mice, indicating mice primarily switch states while located on the side they ultimately choose.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 are supported by choice-oriented occupancy analysis (Figure 9—supplement 1B). The consistent displacement across individual mice strengthens the conclusion. The inference about state switching location (C80) follows logically from the spatial distribution data.

results.result: Investigation downwind of odor ports (where absolute concentration is maximal) is increased on incorrect trials, suggesting mice do not capitalize on absolute concentration information. This pattern contradicts predictions of a single-sniff absolute concentration strategy.
results.evaluation: Claims C86, C96-C97 are supported by lateral occupancy analysis showing incorrect trials have more investigation in regions of high absolute concentration (Figure 10, Figure 1—supplement 2C). This provides additional evidence against absolute concentration strategies and supports gradient-based navigation.

results.result: Both stay and switch trials show increased investigation at and on the unchosen side of midline for correct trials, demonstrating the advantage of midline sampling is not an artifact of trial type asymmetry.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are supported by separate analysis of stay and switch trials (Figure 10—supplement 1). This control addresses a potential confound in the main analysis and strengthens the conclusion about serial-sniff strategy. The consistency across trial types is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Motif transition times indicate 'decision points' at which the animal chooses its next move.
results.evaluation: Claim C78 is a hypothesis proposed by the authors with citation to similar work (Markowitz et al., 2018) but lacks direct experimental validation in this study. While the temporal structure of motif transitions is well-characterized, the interpretation as 'decision points' requires additional evidence such as neural recordings or causal manipulations to be fully supported.

results.result: Summary claims about mice navigating noisy gradients with robust, strategic behavioral programs involving sniff-synchronized movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 are summary statements well-supported by the collective evidence from multiple experiments. These integrate findings from gradient manipulation, perturbation studies, and kinematic analysis. The characterization is accurate and appropriately synthesizes the major findings.

results.result: Background claims about chemotaxis, olfactory navigation strategies across species, and prior work on rodent olfactory behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C24 are background statements supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide context for the current work and accurately represent prior knowledge in the field. The citations appear appropriate and the characterizations are consistent with the cited work.

results.result: Comparative claims about off-axis sampling strategies in bats and olfactory navigation regimes across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C99 and C101-C105 draw comparisons to other sensory systems and species, supported by appropriate citations. The analogy to bat echolocation (C99) is interesting and well-cited. The characterization of different navigation regimes (C102-C105) provides useful context for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: Discussion of prior work on stereo olfaction in odor trail following and mole navigation, including distance-dependent role of stereo vs. serial-sniff cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 accurately represent cited prior work on stereo olfaction and serial-sniff comparisons. These provide important context for interpreting the naris occlusion results and support the authors' hypothesis about task-dependent sensory strategies.

results.result: Discussion claims about task design forcing serial-sniff regime, potential neural mechanisms, limitations of head-fixed studies, and need for naturalistic paradigms.
results.evaluation: Claims C112, C114, C120-C121 are speculative statements about implications and future directions. While C113 and C116-C119 cite relevant prior work, claims about the task forcing a particular regime (C112) or limitations of head-fixed studies (C114, C120) are reasonable inferences but not directly tested. These represent thoughtful discussion but require additional evidence for full support.

results.result: Discussion claims about active sensing, sensorimotor integration, technological advances, and the framework established by this work.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C130 provide appropriate context from prior literature on active sensing and sensorimotor integration. Claims C131-C136 about the contributions of this work are reasonable summaries of the findings. The characterization of the framework (C135-C136) is appropriate given the demonstrated utility of the behavioral analysis methods.
